name: Lubaina Himid
from: Born in Zanzibar in 1954, lives in Preston
about: A cut-out installation that restages Hogarth's satirical paintings with Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan flirting at the centre. In 2017 Himid became the first Black woman to win the Turner Prize.
politics: She asks why Black women have been left out of British history and its galleries, and puts them back in the picture.
lookFor: How she borrows the look of old art to say something about the 1980s.
who: Born in Zanzibar and raised in Britain, she trained in theatre design and became a key figure in the 1980s Black British art movement.
goodAt: Bold colour, humour and putting forgotten people back into history.

name: Kara Walker
about: A 13-metre fountain in Tate Modern's Turbine Hall, built to look like London's Victoria Memorial, but telling the story of the Atlantic slave trade. Walker's silhouettes look sweet and old-fashioned until you see what is happening in them.
politics: Slavery, empire and how countries choose to remember their past with monuments.
lookFor: The gap between the pretty, decorative style and the violence of the story.
who: She grew up in California and Atlanta and became famous in her twenties for room-sized cut-paper silhouettes.
goodAt: Turning a polite, old-fashioned style against the history it hides.

name: Amy Sherald
about: Sherald painted the official portrait of Michelle Obama for the National Portrait Gallery. She paints skin in shades of grey, so you notice the person rather than reading them by their colour.
politics: Who gets painted, and how. Her 2020 portrait of Breonna Taylor, killed by police in Louisville, appeared on the cover of Vanity Fair.
lookFor: The grey skin tones against bright, flat colour and bold clothing.
who: She grew up in Columbus, Georgia, and was working as a waitress while painting before her career took off. She became nationally known with the Michelle Obama portrait.
goodAt: Calm, dignified portraits of everyday Black Americans, with striking colour.

name: Ai Weiwei
about: About 100 million porcelain seeds, each handmade and painted by craftspeople in Jingdezhen, filled the floor of Tate Modern's Turbine Hall. From a distance it looks like one grey mass; up close every seed is different.
politics: The individual and the crowd, mass production and freedom of expression. He was detained by Chinese authorities for 81 days in 2011, and has since made major work about refugees.
lookFor: How one tiny object, repeated, becomes a statement about millions of people.
who: The son of a poet exiled under Mao, he helped design the Beijing Olympic stadium, then became one of China's best-known critics. He now lives in Europe.
goodAt: Huge, simple gestures that carry a political charge, and using social media as art.

name: Banksy
about: Seconds after his painting Girl with Balloon sold at Sotheby's, it shredded itself through a hidden device in the frame. The half-shredded work was renamed and later resold for far more.
politics: War, surveillance, consumerism and the art market itself. He also opened the Walled Off Hotel in Bethlehem, facing the separation wall.
lookFor: How humour makes a serious point travel further.
search: Banksy Love is in the Bin
who: A street artist from Bristol whose identity has never been officially confirmed. He started in the 1990s graffiti scene.
goodAt: Stencils with a single clear joke or message, and stunts that grab headlines.

name: El Anatsui
from: Born in Ghana in 1944, works in Nigeria
about: Enormous shimmering hangings made from thousands of flattened bottle tops from liquor bottles, stitched together with copper wire. They hang like cloth and change shape every time they are installed.
politics: Trade, waste and history. Alcohol was part of the exchange between Europe and West Africa during the slave trade, so the material itself carries that story.
lookFor: How hard metal is made to look as soft as kente cloth.
video: El Anatsui Behind the Red Moon
who: Born in Anyako in the Volta Region of Ghana, he taught for decades at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. He won the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at Venice in 2015.
goodAt: Turning waste into something luxurious, and making sculpture that flows like cloth.

name: Ibrahim Mahama
about: Mahama stitches together hundreds of worn jute sacks, the kind used to carry cocoa and then charcoal in Ghana, and drapes them over whole buildings. He showed this work at the Venice Biennale.
politics: Labour, global trade and who profits from it. He has used his success to build art spaces in Tamale, including the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art.
lookFor: The names, stamps and repairs on each sack: traces of real workers.
who: He studied at KNUST in Kumasi and still works from Tamale in northern Ghana, where he has built studios and art centres.
goodAt: Huge public installations made from materials full of other people's labour.

name: Zanele Muholi
about: An ongoing series of black-and-white portraits of Black lesbian, transgender and gender non-conforming people in South Africa. Muholi calls themself a visual activist rather than an artist.
politics: Visibility and safety for Black LGBTQIA+ people, in a country with a progressive constitution but high levels of hate crime.
lookFor: Direct eye contact: the sitters look back at you as equals.
who: Muholi grew up in Umlazi near Durban and trained at the Market Photo Workshop in Johannesburg. Muholi uses they/them pronouns.
goodAt: Portraits that give people control over how they are seen.

name: Barbara Kruger
about: Bold white words on red bars laid over a woman's face, split into positive and negative. It was made as a poster for a march in support of abortion rights in Washington.
politics: Power, consumerism and control over women's bodies. Her style borrows directly from advertising to turn its methods against it.
lookFor: How few words she needs, and who the 'you' is.
search: Barbara Kruger Your body is a battleground
who: She worked as a graphic designer for magazines like Mademoiselle before turning those skills into art.
goodAt: Short, punchy slogans that look like adverts but question power.

name: Guerrilla Girls
work: Do women have to be naked to get into the Met. Museum?
about: A billboard pointing out that less than 5% of the artists in the Met's modern art sections were women, but 85% of the nudes were female. Members wear gorilla masks and use the names of dead women artists.
politics: Sexism and racism in the art world, backed up by counting.
lookFor: How they use statistics and humour together.
who: An anonymous group of women artists formed in New York in 1985. They have made posters, books and billboards around the world.
goodAt: Using facts, humour and street-style posters to shame institutions into change.

name: Shirin Neshat
from: Born in Iran in 1957, lives in New York
about: Black-and-white photographs of women, often Neshat herself, with Persian poetry written by hand across their skin. She made them after returning to Iran for the first time since the 1979 revolution.
politics: Gender, faith, exile and how women are seen in and outside Iran.
lookFor: Where the writing sits on the body, and how it changes the face or hands.
who: She left Iran to study in the US before the 1979 revolution and could not return for years. She works in photography and film.
goodAt: Powerful black-and-white images about women, faith and exile.

name: JR
about: Huge portraits of Israelis and Palestinians doing the same jobs, pasted side by side on both sides of the separation wall. JR also made the film Faces Places with Agnès Varda, which is on your film list.
politics: Seeing the person on the other side. Close to your debate question.
lookFor: Whether you can tell who is from which side.
who: He started as a teenage graffiti artist in Paris and won the TED Prize in 2011, which funded his global Inside Out project.
goodAt: Huge photographs of ordinary people pasted where you cannot ignore them.

name: Doris Salcedo
about: A long crack running down the floor of Tate Modern's Turbine Hall. Visitors stepped over it and peered in. It was later filled, but the scar is still visible.
politics: Racism, borders and exclusion. Her other work responds to political violence in Colombia, including a floor made from melted guerrilla weapons.
lookFor: How a gap in the floor can feel like a border.
who: She studied in Bogotá and New York and has spent her career responding to violence in Colombia.
goodAt: Quiet, haunting sculpture about loss and the people violence erases.

name: Olafur Eliasson
about: Eliasson brought huge blocks of ice that had broken off the Greenland ice sheet and left them to melt in public squares in Copenhagen, Paris and London. People touched them and watched them disappear.
politics: Climate change, made physical rather than a statistic.
lookFor: People's hands on the ice. The point is to feel it.
who: Born in Denmark to Icelandic parents, he runs a large studio in Berlin. His sun in Tate Modern's Turbine Hall in 2003 drew millions.
goodAt: Using light, water and weather to change how people feel in a space.

name: Mona Hatoum
from: Born in Beirut in 1952 to a Palestinian family, lives in London
about: A steel globe with every continent outlined in buzzing red neon, as if the whole world were a danger zone. Hatoum was stranded in London when war broke out in Lebanon in 1975.
politics: Exile, borders, conflict and the feeling of never being fully at home.
lookFor: How ordinary objects like maps, kitchen tools or beds become threatening.
who: Born in Beirut to a Palestinian family, she was visiting London in 1975 when civil war broke out in Lebanon and stayed.
goodAt: Turning everyday objects into something uneasy or threatening.

name: Faith Ringgold
about: A quilt with a painted scene and handwritten story of a girl in Harlem who dreams of flying over the city from her rooftop. Ringgold turned quilting, often dismissed as craft, into fine art.
politics: Civil rights, Black women's lives and who gets to tell stories in museums.
lookFor: How the text around the edge tells the story alongside the image.
who: She was born in Harlem, taught art in New York schools for years and became a children's author as well as an artist.
goodAt: Story quilts that mix painting, sewing and writing.

name: Sonia Boyce
about: Videos of five Black women singers improvising together, surrounded by golden geometric shapes. Boyce was the first Black woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale, and won its top prize.
politics: Freedom, collaboration and Black British women's voices.
lookFor: Moments when the singers listen to each other.
search: Sonia Boyce Feeling Her Way Venice
who: Born in London to Caribbean parents, she came through the 1980s Black British art movement alongside Lubaina Himid.
goodAt: Collaboration: she builds work with other people rather than alone.

name: Steve McQueen
about: Class photographs of tens of thousands of Year 3 pupils from across London, shown at Tate Britain and on billboards around the city. He also directed Small Axe: Lovers Rock, on your film list.
politics: Who London's future belongs to. A portrait of a whole generation at one moment.
lookFor: Uniforms, poses and who stands where in the class photos.
who: Born in London to Grenadian and Trinidadian parents, he won the Turner Prize in 1999 and an Oscar for 12 Years a Slave.
goodAt: Moving between gallery art and cinema, always with a clear eye on history.

name: Yinka Shonibare
from: Born in London in 1962, grew up in Lagos
about: Thousands of books covered in bright Dutch wax print fabric, with the names of first or second generation immigrants to Britain printed in gold on the spines. He also made the giant ship in a bottle that sat on Trafalgar Square's Fourth Plinth.
politics: Colonialism, migration and what 'British' means. The wax fabric seen as 'African' was first made by the Dutch for the Indonesian market.
lookFor: The names on the spines, and the mix of famous and unknown.
who: Born in London and raised in Lagos, he returned to London to study art. He became a disabled artist after an illness in his teens and works with a team of assistants.
goodAt: Using colourful 'African' fabric to unpick ideas about colonialism and identity.

name: Hew Locke
from: Born in Edinburgh in 1959, grew up in Guyana
about: More than 140 life-size figures marching through Tate Britain, dressed in costumes printed with old share certificates, maps and archive images. It reads like a carnival and a history lesson at once.
politics: Empire, trade and the money that built British institutions, including Tate itself.
lookFor: The details on the costumes: banknotes, company names, faces.
who: Born in Edinburgh, he grew up in Guyana from age five, then returned to Britain to study.
goodAt: Dense, glittering sculpture packed with historical detail.

name: Grayson Perry
about: Six large tapestries following one man as he moves from working class to upper class, told through the things people buy. Perry won the Turner Prize in 2003.
politics: Class and taste in Britain, with humour and affection.
lookFor: Brand names and objects that signal which class each scene belongs to.
video: Grayson Perry Vanity of Small Differences
search: Grayson Perry Vanity of Small Differences tapestry
who: From Chelmsford in Essex, he is a potter, writer and TV presenter, often appearing as his alter ego Claire.
goodAt: Making class and identity funny and approachable, using traditional crafts.

name: Theaster Gates
about: Gates bought an abandoned bank on Chicago's South Side for one dollar and restored it as a library, archive and arts space. He sees fixing buildings as part of his art.
politics: Investment in Black neighbourhoods, and who decides what is worth saving.
lookFor: How the old building and new uses sit together.
search: Theaster Gates Stony Island Arts Bank
who: A potter and urban planner by training, he grew up on Chicago's West Side and works mostly on the South Side.
goodAt: Treating whole buildings and communities as his material.

name: Njideka Akunyili Crosby
from: Born in Nigeria in 1983, lives in Los Angeles
about: A series of portraits of children and young people from her family, in rooms layered with photo transfers from Nigerian magazines and family albums. The patterns pull you in close.
politics: Living between two countries, and what home looks like after migration.
lookFor: The tiny images hidden inside clothes, floors and walls.
search: Njideka Akunyili Crosby The Beautyful Ones
who: She grew up in Enugu and Lagos and moved to the US at 16. Her mother was Dora Akunyili, Nigeria's former Minister of Information.
goodAt: Layered paintings that hold two countries in one room.

name: Cornelia Parker
about: A 13-metre embroidery of the Wikipedia page about Magna Carta, stitched by about 200 people, including prisoners, lawyers, MPs and campaigners. It marked 800 years since the charter.
politics: Rights and who they belong to. Each person chose which words to stitch.
lookFor: Who stitched which words: Edward Snowden stitched 'liberty'.
search: Cornelia Parker Magna Carta An Embroidery
who: She studied in Gloucestershire and Reading and was shortlisted for the Turner Prize in 1997.
goodAt: Taking objects apart, often violently, and rearranging them into something beautiful.

name: Jenny Holzer
about: Short statements like 'Abuse of power comes as no surprise' printed on posters, T-shirts and huge LED signs. Some contradict each other on purpose.
politics: Power, violence and how slogans shape what we believe. Good training for spotting persuasion.
lookFor: Which truisms you agree with, and which ones argue with each other.
who: She started by pasting anonymous posters on New York streets in the late 1970s.
goodAt: Using public language, signs and lights to make people stop and think.
